# Golem: a structured way to build and modularize your app

So far we have only run our app locally in the console. It is time to
build an actual Shiny app! There are multiple ways to do this, but we
will use the package called`golem`.

## Learning objectives

The learning objectives for this session are:

{{< include /includes/objectives/_golem.qmd >}}

::: callout-note
## Reading task: Why golem? \~7 minutes

There are many ways we can make a shiny app. If we want to make a very
simple app and just run it locally, we can just put the code from our
last exercise in a script, source it, and our shiny app will run. Nice
and easy. A more structured way to make a one-script app is by making a
new shiny app project. If we have shiny installed we can go to `file`,
`new project` and select `shiny application`. This creates a one script
app, containing the essentials. Running this app is easy, just click the
`run app` button that appears in your editor or run `shiny::run_app()`
and you are flying. For many apps, this setup is perfectly adequate and
you can deploy it to the internet if you have somewhere to host it.

What then, if our apps are more complex? This is where a package like
`golem` becomes handy. `golem` is a package focused on building a
production-ready, robust shiny app. Once initiated it creates a range of
files that step by step helps you setting up a lot of groundwork so you
don't have to do it later. It helps you setup a github repository and it
can also help you deploy the app to a number of services once you are
done.

One of the most useful features from `golem` is that it natively helps
you modularizing your app. When you modularize you split your app into
smaller components. Suggest you have an app with multiple pages, where
each page provides a different range of buttons, sliders and plots. How
do you keep track of which button leads where? Or what code underlies
which plot? Scripts can easily get out of hand that way, and while we
always think we will be able to understand the code later, this is not
often the case. `golem` makes one script pr. page in your app,
containing info for the UI and server that goes together. So if your app
contains a welcome page, a settings page, and a plot page, `golem` will
make three files for you - a welcome file, a settings file and a plot
file. Additionally it will make a server file and a ui file, where all
your modules are tied together.

Is `golem` overkill for what we are doing here? Certainly! But I want to
introduce it to you already so you know it, and once you start
developing more complex apps, you know where to go.
:::

## Starting a golem

If we want to make a new app and we have golem installed, we can open
the menu and select `new project` (like we did above) and pick
`Package for shiny app using golem`. If we want to do this from the
console, this is also an option, and we will see how this is done below.

Lets make an app about something fun - penguins. We will call it
"penguin app" (or "penguinapp" in R writing)

```{r}
#| eval: false


golem::create_golem(path = "C:/Your_R_projects_destination/penguinapp"
                    )


```

Running this command creates a new R project called penguinapp. We will
see this has quite a few more files than our standard Shiny project.

![Overview of the files created by
golem](/images/golem_files.png){#fig-shiny_ui width="90%"}

This is actually a functional Shiny app, though at this stage it works a
bit differently. We can run it with the command `golem::run_dev()`.
Running this command will take us to a golem welcome page with resources
and information.

To understand what golem really offers, it is beneficial to look at the
dev folder. In this folder we will see three documents:

- 01_start.R
- 02_dev.R
- 03_deploy.R

These three files contains a step by step guide to how you build and
deploy a shiny app. You don't have to do it all (or in the order you are
asked to), but `golem` gives a suggested path through the development
process, starting right after we create our app.

## :speech_balloon: Discussion activity: 01_start.R

**Time: \~5 minutes.**

We don't have time to go too much into detail this session with what you
do in 01_start - but take a few minutes to open the file, and discuss
the content with the person next to you. What kind of information does
`golem` suggest you setup? Do you recognize any terms in this file?

{{< text_snippet sticky_up >}}

`golem` helps you with a lot of housekeeping you usually end up doing
last minutes, including making a DESCRIPTION file (which contains a lot
of input about required packages, info on the author, and whether you
have coined a specific license to the usage of your package.) It also
helps you with a number of other helpful tools for reproducible
development such as using git and github. By doing this ahead of time,
you do all the legwork before development begins, and you won't have to
do it once your app has grown in size.

At this point we will limit ourselves to making a DESCRIPTION file by
running the following:

```{r}
#| eval: false

golem::fill_desc(
  pkg_name = "penguinapp", # The name of the golem package containing the app (typically lowercase, no underscore or periods)
  pkg_title = "PKG_TITLE", # What the Package Does (One Line, Title Case, No Period)
  pkg_description = "PKG_DESC.", # What the package does (one paragraph).
  authors = person(
    given = "AUTHOR_FIRST", # Your First Name
    family = "AUTHOR_LAST", # Your Last Name
    email = "AUTHOR@MAIL.COM", # Your email
    role = c("aut", "cre") # Your role (here author/creator)
  ),
  repo_url = NULL, # The URL of the GitHub repo (optional),
  pkg_version = "0.0.0.9000", # The version of the package containing the app
  set_options = TRUE # Set the global golem options
)
```

A DESCRIPTION file is also where you note what packages are required to
run your app. This can be done by using the function
`usethis::use_package("PACKAGE NAME")` Normally it is sufficient to call
the package on it's own, with a notable exception being the `tidyverse`
package - here you should add the following:
`usethis::use_package("tidyverse", type = "suggests")` because
`tidyverse` is a collection. Adding used packages to the DESCRIPTION
file makes it easier to deploy the app, because it makes it clear what
packages need to be installed on your remote server.

## Development and modularization

We will in this workshop be bad examples and start development on our
penguin app before doing any of the housekeeping. if we are leading by
example, this is a poor example indeed! But jokes aside, our second file
02_dev.R contains the scripts we need to build our app.

There are many different functions in this file and we do not need all
of them - a lot of these functions are advanced edge cases in case you
want to implement specific programs or programming languages. It does
contain some helpful functions:

- usethis::use_github() helps you share your project on github
- usethis::use_data_raw() creates a folder for storing data, and is
  helpful if you want to use data in your app
- golem::add_utils("helpers", with_test = TRUE) creates a script for
  making helper functions, in case you develop your own functions to be
  used in the app

For an in-depth resource about golem see the [following
book](https://engineering-shiny.org/golem.html). Most functionalities
are beyond the scope of this workshop, but we will focus on one:
`golem::add_module()`.

## :speech_balloon: Discussion activity: add_module

**Time: \~5 minutes.**

Open the help page for the add_module() function, using
`?golem::add_module` in the console. Discuss with the person next to you
what it does, and why this could be useful

## Making our first module

We want to make an app about the `penguins` dataset. In general, it is
considered good design form to consider what the app should look like
before we start coding. It can often be beneficial to start drawing the
UI on a pice of paper. However, we do not have the time for this today.
Lets take a look at the data and see what we can do with it:

```{r}
dplyr::slice_head(penguins,n = 10)
```

We see we have eight different columns with data about the penguins -
species, island, bill length, etc. Lets make a module called "overview"
where we will make a an explorative plot in the next chapter. For now,
we build the module:

```{r}
#| eval: false

golem::add_module(name = "overview")

```

you will notice the standard golem output includes an argument stating
`with_test=TRUE`. This is not necessary for our app, and truth being
told I have yet to grasp the potential and utility in the tests offered
by golem. Know they are there, and you can look for information if this
is of interest to you.

If we run this command, we should now get a new file - we get a console
output stating `File created at R/mod_overview.R`. Looking in our R
folder we see there now is a script called mod_overview.R. The script
contains several chunks - lets go through them in turn

```{r}
#| eval: false
mod_overview_ui <- function(id) {
  ns <- NS(id)
  tagList(
 
  )
}

```

This first chunk is the UI component. In the function called `tagList`
(from shiny) we can add all the UI components we desire - cards, pages,
you name it. As a general rule, whenever you have more than one element,
it is a good idea to add them in the `tagList` function. For now, the UI
is empty.

Next thing we see is the server:

```{r}
#| eval: false
mod_overview_server <- function(id){
  moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session){
    ns <- session$ns
 
  })
}

```

In this, we put the server component in. So far, this is very similar to
our initial example of a Shiny app. The next part is commented out (with
#) but is quite interesting:

```{r}
#| eval: false

## To be copied in the UI
# mod_overview_ui("overview_1")
    
## To be copied in the server
# mod_overview_server("overview_1")

```

`golem` gives us to two functions we can paste into our UI and server
script. These are found in the /R folder and are called "app_ui" and
"app_server". If we open app_ui we will see the following in the top
part:

```{r}
#| eval: false

app_ui <- function(request) {
  tagList(
    # Leave this function for adding external resources
    golem_add_external_resources(),
    # Your application UI logic
    fluidPage(
      golem::golem_welcome_page() # Remove this line to start building your UI
    )
  )
}

```

Here we see the description of the UI - it describes the `golem` demo
page we saw before, with all the golem resources. Standard is
`shiny::fluidPage`, but if you want to use `bslib` as we discussed in
the previous chapter, it is worth upgrading the page type to a one from
this package - the equivalent is `bslib::page_fluid()`. Using the
default `shiny::fluidPage` can cause some unexpected interactions with
`bslib elements`.

In this case, we like the `golem` page, but we want to make a page of
our own. We will turn it into a page with a navigation bar, and add our
new module. We replace `fluidPage` with `bslib::page_navbar()`, and wrap
the `golem_welcome_page()` in `bslib::nav_panel()`, telling shiny that
we want it to be displayed as a panel in the navigation bar. We also
give a title for the tab.

Then we copy the text from the golem module
(`mod_overview_ui("overview_1")`) into another `nav_panel()` instance,
and gives it a title.

```{r}
#| eval: false

app_ui <- function(request) {
  tagList(
    # Leave this function for adding external resources
    golem_add_external_resources(),
    # Your application UI logic
    bslib::page_navbar(
      bslib::nav_panel(
        title = "golem welcome page",
        golem::golem_welcome_page()
      ),
      bslib::nav_panel(
        title = "Our awesome penguin app",
        mod_overview_ui("overview_1")
      )
       
    )
  )
}

```

Next, we open the app_server script. We see it is currently empty - the
welcome page is apparantly all UI and no server. We want to add a server
of our own, and copy the server script from our module file
(`mod_overview_server("overview_1")`)

```{r}
#| eval: false
app_server <- function(input, output, session) {
  # Your application server logic
  mod_overview_server("overview_1")
}

```

if we run `golem::run_dev()` we will now get an app with two tabs - the
golem page and an empty page. We have made a modularized app! additional
modules can be added the same way, and the scripts kept to a manageable
size. Note that the background is purple, which is being hard set by the
golem welcome page - if we delete that page it will go away.

## Reading activity: 03_deploy.R

**Time: \\3 minutes.**

In our dev folder we had a final file - 03_deploy.R. This one contains
helper functions for when your app is ready to be shared with the world.
it helps you build functions from your app into a package (and helps you
check if it is good enough to be added to CRAN, where we download our
packages from), and it contains a number of options to help prepare your
app to be hosted on platforms such as posit connect or other platforms.
Deploying is beyond the scope of this workshop, but this file will give
you a number of options you can look up and find a solution that works
for you. If you want an easy way to share apps, I encourage you to check
out [posit connect cloud](https://connect.posit.cloud/) - they have free
plans if your app is small, and once your account is connected, it
requires few steps to upload and update apps.

{{< text_snippet sticky_up >}}

## Summary

You have now learned

- How to build an app with golem

- How the dev files work

- How modularization works

- Where you can find information about how to share your app with the
  world
